output.title: Treat data cleaning as a workflow boundary, not a feature
output.body:
If you run a small business, data cleaning is usually not the real decision. The decision is whether a recurring workflow only works if the input data is clean enough to trust. That is a design constraint, not a tool choice.

Start with one workflow you repeat every week: invoices, customer records, or form replies. Then write down the input structure and the quality rule that matters before anything downstream happens. For example, you might require invoice amount, supplier, and reference to match before a human approves it. That is not a promise of automation; it is the boundary that tells you whether automation is even sensible.

If the data arrives in a predictable format and the success rule is clear, AI can sit inside a controlled process with human review. If the data is messy and the success rule is vague, manual cleaning or no automation at all is the more honest answer. In that case, the problem is not that the model is weak. It is that the workflow has no stable rulebook.

That is how we frame the working examples we built: the knowledge assistant works with approved material, and the accounts-payable demo uses checks and human-only approval on synthetic data. Both are self-built demos, not customer case studies. The accounts-payable demo also shows arithmetic checks, duplicate blocking, and refusal of agent approval attempts; it does not include OCR or three-way matching.

A useful next step is simple: ask yourself, does this workflow happen the same way every week, and can I write the quality rules in plain English?
